source.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
source.authors: Li-Wei Wang; Lunjia Hu; Jiayuan Gu; Zhi-Qiang Hu; Y. Wu; Kun He; J. Hopcroft

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary sections are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures representation matches across independently initialized networks and reports low similarity in most convolutional layers, qualifying the expectation of convergent learning. It also gives input/output alignment as an explanation for higher similarity near those layers.
record.gate_note: The text reports validation accuracies and discusses figures, but accuracy is not a representation-match result. Detailed per-layer curves are plotted without numerical values; rows below record the authors' explicit qualitative summaries rather than inventing per-layer values. The simple-match figures include plotted distributions; the text describes them qualitatively as having few small matches.
record.test_reason: The study trains five differently seeded copies each of VGG11/13/16 and ResNet18/34 on CIFAR10, plus VGG16 on ImageNet. It measures neuron-activation subspace matches between same-layer neurons. It reports very low matching in most convolutional layers, a result against convergent learning across seeds (V3). It argues that higher similarity near the input and output comes from alignment to the shared input and output (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find convolutional-layer representations of differently initialized same-architecture networks much less similar than expected, in terms of subspace match. They attribute boundary-layer similarity to input or output alignment. They leave open whether the networks learn different representations or subspace match is a poor metric.
record.recipe_differences: Uses neuron activation vectors and approximate subspace matches, rather than the earlier study's heuristic one-to-one and cluster correspondence analyses. It studies same-architecture networks with different initializations.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity differs by layer location: most convolutional layers have low matches, while layers near input or output can show higher overall similarity. The study also reports results across datasets, architectures, and epsilon values, but does not establish a numerical dependence on those choices in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Two untrained networks drawn from the same initialization distribution show some subspace match. A network after training is much less similar to its own untrained state.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some measured representational similarity reflects shared initialization distributions rather than learned convergence.

record.problems: The empirical similarity evidence is specific to same-architecture CNNs and activation-subspace matching. Many results are presented only in figures, without numerical tables or uncertainty estimates. The study does not compare alternative similarity metrics, and the authors themselves question whether subspace match is an adequate metric.
record.rows_left_out: Per-layer values in Figure 1 and supplementary Figure 3, and the full plotted distributions in Figure 2, are not transcribed because the text provides no numerical values for them. The qualitative aggregate and the simple-match outcomes explicitly described in the text are retained. Other figure-only per-architecture or per-layer outcomes are not separately represented.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep. No comparison across architectures, objectives or data. Only same-architecture pairs are compared.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption data.
No stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping. The epsilon-subspace match is related to linear reconstructability, but no mapping loss is reported.
No test of recurring interpretable features or circuits. Appendix E.4 only visualizes two small simple matches qualitatively.

No comparison of similarity measures or out-of-distribution inputs. The authors only raise the question of whether subspace match is a good metric. Epsilon is varied, but its effect is shown only in figures.

missing.what: ImageNet-VGG16, a lower-accuracy run, shows no similarity in layers near the output. This contrasts with the CIFAR runs and ties output-layer similarity to accuracy.
Per-architecture results for VGG11/13/16 on CIFAR10 are described as similar to the main results. They are not separate rows.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. Rows r6 and r7 were unlinked from V7. The authors' doubt about the metric bears on V6 only as an argument, not a measured comparison. Li et al. 2016 (an original V3 source) found shared core features with correlation measures, so the contrast hints at metric dependence, but the study does not test it. All quantitative curves are figure-only and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, and no comparison of models differing in architecture, objective, training data, or modality.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language models.

Tests same-architecture networks trained from different random initializations using activation-subspace matches. Does not test whether individual interpretable features recur, or whether the results hold for other similarity measures.
Does not test mapping representations between models with little loss, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.
Uses activation-subspace match with varying error tolerance and validation inputs, but does not compare similarity measures or report out-of-distribution results.

Reports partial similarity and discusses shared input/output alignment as an explanation near boundary layers. Does not vary shared training data or objectives, test a common model of reality, or measure a scale-related plateau.

rows.subject: Differently initialized networks (aggregate across the tested CNN experiments)
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum matching similarity between same-layer neuron activation subspaces.

conditions.value: VGG and ResNet on CIFAR10 and ImageNet experiments
various; exact values not stated here

rows.value: Very low for most convolutional layers; almost zero for deep networks.
rows.uncertainty: Little variance among different network pairs, as stated by the authors; numerical uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: Qualitative aggregate statement; the paper does not provide numerical values in the text for each layer or architecture. The authors characterize the low match as contrary to prevalent expectation.
rows.check: For V3 the state is absent: maximum matching similarity is 'very low' in most conv layers and 'almost zero' for deep networks. For V7 the same result means alignment is far from complete, i.e. V7's incompleteness is observed. Per-layer and per-epsilon values are figure-only.

source_check.correct: Separate version-specific states: absent for V3 under this measure; observed for V7's incomplete-alignment component.
source_check.problem: The shared absent state reverses the interpretation for V7: very low alignment supports incomplete convergence.

rows.subject: Differently initialized networks (aggregate across the tested CNN experiments)
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum matching similarity between same-layer neuron activation subspaces.
rows.value: Relatively high similarity; authors attribute it to alignment to the same input data and low dimensionality of early layers.
rows.note: The authors describe this as an input-alignment/low-dimensionality effect, not evidence of intrinsically shared intermediate representations.
rows.check: Overall similarity is relatively high near the input. The authors attribute it to alignment with the same input and low dimensionality, not shared learned features. Simple-match analysis (r4) shows lower similarity in the finer structure.

rows.subject: Differently initialized networks (aggregate across the tested CNN experiments)
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum matching similarity between same-layer neuron activation subspaces.

conditions.value: high accuracy in the experiments where output-adjacent similarity is reported

rows.value: Sometimes high; the authors attribute it to alignment to the output.
rows.note: The authors also note an experiment with relatively low accuracy in which output-adjacent layers do not show similarity.
rows.check: Similarity near the output is only 'sometimes' high and is attributed to output alignment. It is absent in the lower-accuracy ImageNet-VGG16 run (Fig 1b), which deserves its own row.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, conclusion 2; Figure 1(b); supplementary Section E.3.

rows.subject: Differently initialized network pair (the pair used for the simple-match illustration)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the distribution of simple-match sizes between same-layer activations.
rows.value: Few simple matches with small sizes.
rows.note: The plotted distribution is not numerically tabulated; the paper explicitly states that few small simple matches occur.
rows.check: The maximum match near the input is 44 neurons at epsilon 0.3, with few small simple matches. Little shared structure appears at fine granularity. The layer width is not stated, so the fraction matched cannot be computed.

rows.subject: Differently initialized network pair (the pair used for the simple-match illustration)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the distribution of simple-match sizes between same-layer activations.
rows.value: Few simple matches with small sizes, despite relatively high overall similarity.
rows.note: The plotted distribution is not numerically tabulated; the paper explicitly states that few small simple matches occur.
rows.check: The layer near the output has a maximum match of 118 at epsilon 0.152. Simple matches are all large (about 85–110 neurons), so the shared subspace is distributed with no small shared features. The authors read this as output alignment, not intrinsic shared representation.

rows.subject: Two untrained networks using the same distribution for random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum matching similarity between networks at initialization.
rows.value: Some similarity, as described by the authors; numerical values are figure-only.
rows.note: The authors suggest that similarity may result from both networks drawing parameters from the same distributions.
rows.check: This compares two untrained networks; it is a baseline about initialization similarity, not convergence of trained models. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Untrained network compared with the same network after fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum matching similarity across training stages.
rows.value: Much more different from one another than the two untrained networks; numerical values are figure-only.
rows.note: The authors state that the untrained and trained networks are much more different; the plotted values are not tabulated.
rows.check: This compares the same network before and after training, not independently trained models. It does not measure cross-model convergence.

relationships.condition: Intermediate convolutional layers of seed-varied VGG/ResNet on CIFAR10 and ImageNet, under subspace match
relationships.reason: Maximum matching similarity is very low in most conv layers and near zero in deep networks, with little variance across pairs (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Maximum matching similarity was very low in most convolutional layers and near zero in deep networks, with little variation across seed pairs.

relationships.condition: Layers close to the input or output
relationships.reason: Some overall subspace match exists, but it is attributed to input or output alignment. Only large simple matches occur, and output-layer match vanishes at low accuracy (r2, r3, r4, r5).

source_check.reason: r2–r5 show boundary-layer similarity with input/output explanations, accuracy dependence, and little fine-grained matching. The rationale should say very few small simple matches, rather than only large matches.

relationships.reason: Alignment is far from complete (r1). Where it is higher, the authors attribute it to the shared input data and the shared output objective (r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Subspace alignment remained far from complete, and the authors attributed greater similarity to shared input data and output objectives.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: r1 supports incomplete alignment; r2–r3 support the authors' shared-input and output-alignment explanations. Scaling plateaus and competing reality-based explanations are untested.
